articles.author: Engroso
articles.description:
Traditionally, experimenting with images or videos involved generating and storing several versions, which can take time and storage space. Every new campaign or test variation meant uploading new files, which slows down creative workflows and clutters storage systems.
This approach doesn’t scale well in a world where businesses must adapt quickly to trends, user behavior, or personalization strategies.
Dynamic URLs allow teams to apply on-the-fly transformations to media assets using URL parameters. By simply modifying the URL, one file can serve endless variants. It can be resized, cropped, filtered, overlaid with text, or stylized, making experimentation both fast and lightweight.
By leveraging this, developers, marketers, and content creators can instantly test different layouts, formats, and styles. Creative teams can experiment without waiting on developers or file uploads. Developers can build systems that automatically tailor content based on user context, like device type, location, or preferences, by dynamically modifying URLs at runtime.

E-commerce: Show personalized product images with region-specific prices or seasonal backgrounds.
Media & Publishing: Optimize images for different screen sizes and orientations.
Marketing Teams: Run quick visual tests with different headlines, CTAs, or badges without creating new assets.
Dynamic URLs unlock a faster, more efficient way to experiment with media. By shifting from static assets to flexible, on-demand transformations, teams can iterate quickly, reduce storage clutter, and deliver personalized experiences at scale.
Cloudinary’s Dynamic URLs offer a powerful way to test, iterate, and optimize visual assets without creating multiple static versions.
articles.title: How Dynamic URLs Help You Test Content at Scale

(aka: “Giving numbers and strings meaningful values for your app.”)
You’re making a game with four difficulties:
Easy
Medium
Hard
Impossible
You could:
Use "easy", "medium", etc. everywhere (but risk typos like "medum")
Use numbers like 1, 2, 3, 4 (but you’ll forget which is which)
Enums help you give names to these values and keep them organized.
An Enum is like a labeled list of values you can use in your code.
